title: A Beautiful Whorl
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2985, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 2985 · constellation Ursa Major · about 70 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Several tightly wound spiral arms widen as they curl out from the bright core of NGC 2985, fading gradually until they disappear into the emptiness of intergalactic space. The galaxy's nearly perfect symmetry hints at its complex structure.
Galaxies come in many shapes and sizes, and the spiral is one of the key types. NGC 2985 lies roughly 70 million light-years from the Solar System, in the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear.

Spirals do not always stay that way. Over very long spans of time, spiral galaxies tend to run into other galaxies, and these encounters often end in mergers. The collisions jumble the winding structures of the original galaxies, smoothing out and rounding their shapes. The resulting galaxies have a beauty of their own, quite different from the spirals they came from.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.57 x 1.75 arcminutes) and distance (70 million light years), the frame spans roughly 32,000 × 36,000 light-years. Its light set out about 70 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 2985 through a narrow filter at 658 nm and a filter at 814 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can, tracing the faint outer arms as they fade.
